cues.text: Tom, could I ask you for some advice, please?
cues.speaker: HAZEL

cues.text: Yes of course, if you think I can help. What’s it about?
cues.speaker: TOM

cues.text: It’s my first media studies assignment, and I’m not sure how to go about it. You must have done it last year.
cues.speaker: HAZEL

cues.text: Is that the one comparing the coverage of a particular story in a range of newspapers?
cues.speaker: TOM

cues.text: That’s right.
cues.speaker: HAZEL

cues.text: Oh yes, I really enjoyed writing it.
cues.speaker: TOM

cues.text: So what sort of things do I need to compare?
cues.speaker: HAZEL

cues.text: Well, there are several things. For example, there’s the question of which page of the newspaper the item appears on.
cues.speaker: TOM

cues.text: You mean, because there’s a big difference between having it on the front page and the bottom of page ten, for instance?
cues.speaker: HAZEL

cues.text: Exactly. And that shows how important the editor thinks the story is. Then there’s the size – how many column inches the story is given, how many columns it spreads over.
cues.speaker: TOM

cues.text: And I suppose that includes the headline.
cues.speaker: HAZEL

cues.text: It certainly does. It’s all part of attracting the reader’s attention.
cues.speaker: TOM

cues.text: What about graphics – whether there’s anything visual in addition to the text?
cues.speaker: HAZEL

cues.text: Yes, you need to consider those, too, because they can have a big effect on the reader’s understanding of the story – sometimes a bigger effect than the text itself. Then you’ll need to look at how the item is put together: what structure is it given?
cues.speaker: TOM

cues.text: Bear in mind that not many people read beyond the first paragraph, so what has the journalist put at the beginning? And if, say, three are conflicting opinions about something, does one appear near the end, where people probably won’t read it?
cues.speaker: TOM

cues.text: And newspapers sometimes give wrong or misleading information, don’t they?
cues.speaker: HAZEL

cues.text: Yes, if you can. Compare what’s in different versions, and as far as possible, try and work out what’s true and what isn’t. And that relates to a very important point: what’s the writer’s purpose, or at least the most important one, if they have several.
cues.speaker: TOM

cues.text: It may seem to be to inform the public, but often it’s that they want to create fear, or controversy, or to make somebody look ridiculous.
cues.speaker: TOM

cues.text: Gosh, I see what you mean. And I suppose the writer may make assumptions about the reader.
cues.speaker: HAZEL

cues.text: That’s right – about their knowledge of the subject, their attitudes, and their level of education, which means writing so that the readers understand without feeling patronised. All of that will make a difference to how story is presented.
cues.speaker: TOM

cues.text: Does it matter what type of story I write about?
cues.speaker: HAZEL

cues.text: No – national or international politics, the arts … Anything, as long as it’s covered in two or three newspaper. Though of course it’ll be easier and more fun if it’s something you’re interested in and know something about.
cues.speaker: TOM

cues.text: And on that basis a national news item would be worth analysing – I’m quite keen on politics, so I’ll try and find a suitable topic. What did you choose for your analysis, Tom?
cues.speaker: HAZEL

cues.text: I was interested in how newspapers express their opinions explicitly, so I wanted to compare editorials in different papers, but when I started looking. I couldn’t find two on the same topic that I felt like analysing.
cues.speaker: TOM

cues.text: In that case, I won’t even bother to look.
cues.speaker: HAZEL

cues.text: So in the end I chose a human interest story – a terribly emotional story about a young girl who was very ill, and lots of other people – mostly strangers – raised money so she could go abroad for treatment.
cues.speaker: TOM

cues.text: Actually, I was surprised – some papers just wrote about how wonderful everyone was, but others considered the broader picture, like why treatment wasn’t available here.
cues.speaker: TOM

cues.text: Hmm, I usually find stories like that raise quite strong feelings in me! I’ll avoid that . Perhaps I’ll choose an arts topic, like different reviews of a film, or something about funding for the arts – I’ll think about that.
cues.speaker: HAZEL

cues.text: Yes, that might be interesting.
cues.speaker: TOM

cues.text: OK, well thanks a lot for your help, Tom. It’s been really useful.
cues.speaker: HAZEL

cues.text: You’re welcome. Good luck with the assignment, Hazel.
cues.speaker: TOM
